elements.section: Manage anaphylaxis and refer urgently:
elements.text: Manage anaphylaxis and refer urgently:

elements.section: Manage anaphylaxis and refer urgently:
elements.text: Give immediately adrenaline2 0.5mL (1:1000 solution) IM into mid outer thigh. Repeat every 5 minutes if needed. If patient has a prescribed auto-injector (like EpiPen®) available, use instead.

elements.section: Manage anaphylaxis and refer urgently:
elements.text: Raise legs and give face mask oxygen at 8-10L/min up to 15L/min (100%) if needed.

elements.section: Manage anaphylaxis and refer urgently:
elements.text: Give sodium chloride 0.9% 1-2 L IV rapidly if BP still < 90/60 after adrenaline. Repeat until systolic BP > 90 then continue 1L 6 hourly. Stop if breathing worsens.

elements.section: Manage anaphylaxis and refer urgently:
elements.text: If persistent wheeze or difficulty breathing despite adrenaline2, also give 1mL salbutamol 0.5% solution and 2mL ipratropium bromide solution with 1mL sodium chloride 0.9% via nebuliser every 20 minutes for 3 doses. If needed, assess and manage airway 16.

elements.section: Manage anaphylaxis and refer urgently:
elements.text: Give hydrocortisone 200mg IM/slow IV immediately and promethazine 50mg IM/slow IV.

Advise the patient with previous anaphylaxis • Advise to avoid identified trigger/s and if trigger is a medication, to always inform health worker. • Ensure patient has a plan in case of anaphylaxis: ambulance telephone number, nearest hospital and reliable transport plan. • If adrenaline2 auto-injector device (like EpiPen®) prescribed, ensure patient knows when and how to use it: - If exposed to trigger, use immediately if any of: itch/rash, face/tongue swelling, itchy/tight throat, cough, wheeze, difficulty breathing, dizziness/collapse, abdominal pain or vomiting. After use,
immediately phone for ambulance. - Advise to read instructions found in packaging. • Arrange a MedicAlert® bracelet 200 and advise patient to always wear it.
Assess the patient with previous anaphylaxis
Assess When to assess Note
Trigger At first visit Ensure a specialist has reviewed the patient with anaphylaxis to confirm trigger/s. Common triggers include medications, food1 and insect bites/stings.

Other allergy At first visit • If recurrent cough, wheeze, tight chest or difficulty breathing, exclude asthma 138. If known asthma, give routine asthma care 140. • If patches of dry, scaly, itchy skin on wrists, ankles, inside elbows or behind knees, eczema likely 84. • If itchy, red, raised wheals that appear suddenly and usually disappear within 24 hours, urticaria likely 84. • If recurrent sneezing or itchy/runny/blocked nose most days for > 4 weeks, allergic rhinitis likely 51. • If both eyes watery and itchy, allergic conjunctivitis likely 48.
1Common foods causing anaphylaxis include peanuts, tree nuts, egg, milk and fish. 2Adrenaline is also known as epinephrine.
